t: The Number of Passengers in Each Bus I — Interval Join via LAG
o: Each passenger boards the first bus arriving at or after their own arrival time, so bus k serves exactly the waiting passengers whose arrival lies after the previous bus's arrival and no later than its own. Walking example 1: bus 1 (time 2) takes passenger 11 (arrived 1); bus 2 (time 4) finds nobody because passengers 12, 13 and 14 arrive at times 5, 6 and 7; bus 3 (time 7) collects 12, 13 and 14 — producing counts 1, 0, 3. The relational formulation gives each bus its predecessor's arrival time with the LAG window function, then LEFT JOINs Passengers on the half-open interval (prev_time, arrival_time]; the LEFT JOIN preserves buses with zero passengers, which COUNT(passenger_id) reports as 0.
k: A passenger is available to a bus exactly when their arrival falls in the interval (previous bus time, this bus time] — anyone earlier already boarded.
LAG(arrival_time) OVER (ORDER BY arrival_time) supplies each bus's predecessor in one pass.
LEFT JOIN plus COUNT(passenger_id) yields 0 for empty buses; COUNT(*) would wrongly report 1.

a.n: Approach 1: LAG Window + Half-Open Interval LEFT JOIN
a.i: Order buses by arrival time and attach prev_time via LAG. Passenger p rides bus b iff p.arrival_time <= b.arrival_time AND (b.prev_time IS NULL OR p.arrival_time > b.prev_time). Grouping by bus_id and counting passenger ids produces the required table ordered by bus_id.
s: Build a CTE adding prev_time = LAG(arrival_time) OVER (ORDER BY arrival_time) to every bus.
LEFT JOIN Passengers with the interval condition above.
Group by bus_id and select COUNT(p.passenger_id) AS passengers_cnt.
Order the result by bus_id ascending.

c.python:
# Database problem — the accepted submission is a single MySQL query:
WITH bounds AS (
    SELECT bus_id,
           arrival_time,
           LAG(arrival_time) OVER (ORDER BY arrival_time) AS prev_time
    FROM Buses
)
SELECT b.bus_id,
       COUNT(p.passenger_id) AS passengers_cnt
FROM bounds b
LEFT JOIN Passengers p
       ON p.arrival_time <= b.arrival_time
      AND (b.prev_time IS NULL OR p.arrival_time > b.prev_time)
GROUP BY b.bus_id
ORDER BY b.bus_id ASC;

a.n: Approach 2: Correlated NOT EXISTS Guard (No Window Functions)
a.i: On engines without LAG, encode the boarding greediness directly: passenger p may ride bus b only if no third bus arrived in [p.arrival_time, b.arrival_time) — such a bus would have taken p first. The anti-existence subquery expresses this without any window machinery and is robust to negative timestamps.
s: LEFT JOIN Passengers p ON p.arrival_time <= b.arrival_time.
Add AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Buses other WHERE other.arrival_time >= p.arrival_time AND other.arrival_time < b.arrival_time).
Group by bus_id, count passenger ids.

c.python:
# Database problem — the accepted submission is a single MySQL query:
SELECT b.bus_id,
       COUNT(p.passenger_id) AS passengers_cnt
FROM Buses b
LEFT JOIN Passengers p
       ON p.arrival_time <= b.arrival_time
      AND NOT EXISTS (
            SELECT 1 FROM Buses other
            WHERE other.arrival_time >= p.arrival_time
              AND other.arrival_time < b.arrival_time
      )
GROUP BY b.bus_id
ORDER BY b.bus_id ASC;

w: Frame the problem as intervals first — it converts the greedy boarding story into a single join condition. Pitfalls: INNER JOIN silently drops empty buses (bus 2 must appear with 0), COUNT(*) miscounts them as 1, and using a non-strict comparison against prev_time lets passengers board twice (bus 3 would wrongly claim passenger 11 as well). The premium Part II adds bus capacity constraints, turning this into a sequential assignment problem better solved procedurally or with running sums.
